content_voiceover: This is the master regulatory diagram for hepcidin, arguably the single most testable molecule in iron physiology. Hepcidin is produced by the liver and acts as a negative iron regulator, it binds ferroportin on macrophages and duodenal enterocytes, triggering its degradation and blocking iron release into plasma. Hepcidin rises with increased iron levels and with inflammation via IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha, that's the mechanism behind anemia of inflammation, iron gets trapped inside macrophages. Hepcidin falls with iron deficiency, hypoxia, and increased erythropoiesis, mediated by HIF-2 alpha driving EPO and erythroferrone, which suppresses hepcidin to feed the marrow with iron. This same erythroferrone-driven suppression explains the iron overload seen in thalassemia even without transfusions. Genetically, loss of function in the iron sensor complex, HJV, HFE, TfR2, or in TMPRSS6, causes hereditary hemochromatosis by failing to raise hepcidin appropriately. And renal dysfunction decreases hepcidin clearance, contributing to iron dysregulation in chronic kidney disease. Know this pathway cold, it's the mechanistic backbone for therapies like luspatercept and hepcidin modulators.
keypoints: Hepcidin = negative iron regulator (liver-derived); binds & degrades ferroportin
↑Hepcidin: iron overload, inflammation (IL-1/6, TNF-α) → anemia of inflammation
Erythroferrone-mediated hepcidin suppression → iron overload in thalassemia (no transfusion needed)
keypoint_voiceover: The single most important fact: hepcidin degrades ferroportin, so high hepcidin blocks iron release, causing anemia of inflammation, while low hepcidin, driven by erythroferrone in ineffective erythropoiesis, explains iron overload in thalassemia. And remember, loss of function in HFE, hemojuvelin, TfR2, or TMPRSS6 causes hereditary hemochromatosis by failing to appropriately raise hepcidin.
